At last, “Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay,” was formally charged.

His judges sat on the bench in feathered hats, but elsewhere rough red caps and tricolor cockades predominated. Surveying the jury and the disorderly audience, he might have thought that the normal order had been overturned and criminals were now trying honest men. The lowest, cruelest, and most vicious elements of a city that had always possessed its share of them controlled the proceedings. Unchecked, they shouted comments, applauded, condemned, anticipated the outcome, and pressed for it to arrive. Most of the men carried weapons of one kind or another. Some women wore knives, others daggers; some ate and drank while watching, and many knitted. One of the knitters kept a spare piece of work tucked under her arm. She sat in a front row beside a man he had not seen since arriving at the Barrier, but whom he immediately remembered as Defarge. He noticed her whisper into the man's ear once or twice and supposed that she was his wife. Most striking, however, was that although the pair had placed themselves as close to him as they could, they never looked towards him. They seemed to await something with stubborn determination, keeping their eyes on the jury alone. Below the President sat Doctor Manette in his usual understated clothes. As far as the prisoner could tell, the Doctor and Mr. Lorry were the only men there outside the Tribunal who wore their ordinary clothing instead of adopting the rough dress of the Carmagnole.

The public prosecutor accused Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay, of being an emigrant whose life was forfeit to the Republic under the decree banishing all emigrants on pain of death. That the decree had been issued after his return to France meant nothing. The prisoner was there, and so was the decree. He had been caught in France, and his head was demanded.

“Off with his head!” the audience cried. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to silence them and asked whether the prisoner had, in fact, lived in England for many years.

Without question, he had.

Was he not an emigrant, then? What did he consider himself?

He hoped he was not an emigrant according to the meaning and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President asked.

Because he had freely renounced a title and a social position he found objectionable, and had left his country—before, he pointed out, the word “emigrant” carried its present meaning in the Tribunal—to earn his living through his own work in England, rather than through the labor of France's overburdened people.

Well, I told him I needed the watermelon. But he said I hadn't needed it to escape from prison, and that was the difference. If I'd wanted to hide a knife inside it and sneak it to Jim so he could kill the castle steward, that would have been all right. I let the matter drop. Still, I couldn't see the benefit of pretending to be a prisoner if I had to sit and puzzle over such fancy little differences every time I got a chance to grab a watermelon.

Anyway, as I was saying, that morning we waited until everyone had settled down to work and the yard was empty. Then Tom took the sack into the lean-to while I stood some distance away to keep watch. After a while he came out, and we sat on the woodpile to talk.

“Everything's taken care of except the tools,” he said. “And that's easy to fix.”

“Tools?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“What kind of tools?”

“Digging tools, of course. We're not going to chew him out, are we?”

“Aren't those old broken picks and things in there good enough to dig Jim out with?” I asked.

He turned towards me with a look of pity that could almost make you cry.

“Huck Finn, have you ever heard of a prisoner with picks, shovels, and every modern convenience in his cupboard to help him dig his way out? Tell me, if you've got any sense at all, how could he become a hero that way? They might as well lend him the key and be done with it. Picks and shovels! They wouldn't give those to a king.”

“Well, if we don't want picks and shovels,” I said, “what do we want?”

“A couple of table knives.”

“To dig underneath that cabin's foundations?”

“Yes.”

“Damn it, Tom, that's foolish.”

“It doesn't matter how foolish it is. It's the right way, and the usual way. I've never heard of any other way, and I've read all the books that explain these things. They always dig out with a table knife. And not through dirt, either—usually through solid rock. It takes weeks and weeks, practically forever. Think of that prisoner in the lowest dungeon of Castle Deef, in Marseilles harbor, who dug himself out like that. How long do you suppose it took him?”

“I don't know.”

“Well, guess.”

“I don't know. A month and a half.”

I don't want to get mixed up in anything like that, I told myself.

When I came downstairs that morning, the parlor was closed and the people who had kept watch were gone. Nobody was around except the family, the widow Bartley, and our bunch. I studied their faces to see whether anything had happened, but I couldn't tell.

Around noon the undertaker arrived with his assistant. They placed the coffin on two chairs in the middle of the room, arranged all our other chairs in rows, and borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were full. The coffin lid looked just as it had before, but with people around I didn't dare look underneath it.

Then everyone began arriving. The swindlers and the girls sat in the front row at the head of the coffin. For half an hour the visitors moved slowly past in single file, each looking down for a moment at the dead man's face, with some dropping a tear into the coffin. Everything was quiet and solemn, except for the girls and the swindlers holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bowed, and sobbing a little. The only other sounds were feet scraping the floor and people blowing their noses, which they always do more at funerals than anywhere except church.

Once the rooms were packed, the undertaker glided about in his black gloves, quietly soothing everyone, making final adjustments, and getting people and things settled comfortably into place. He made no more noise than a cat. Without speaking, he moved people around, squeezed in late arrivals, and opened pathways through the crowd, directing it all with nods and hand gestures. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the quietest, smoothest, sneakiest-moving man I'd ever seen, and he had about as much of a smile as a ham.

They had borrowed a small reed organ, and it was a sickly one. When everything was ready, a young woman sat down to play. It squeaked and groaned as if its stomach hurt. Everybody joined in the singing, and as far as I was concerned, Peter was the only one getting a good deal. Then the Reverend Hobson began speaking, slowly and solemnly. Immediately the most outrageous racket anyone ever heard broke out in the cellar. It was only one dog, but he made an incredible noise and kept it going without a pause. The minister had to stand over the coffin and wait. You couldn't hear yourself think.
